world_behind.title: The child of the worst years
world_behind.text: Joseph was born "in the days of my greatest sorrow" (v. 1): somewhere in the eight-year desert stretch that killed Ishmael, broke the bows, and nearly starved the camp. Lehi names the era "the wilderness of mine afflictions" (v. 1) and gives the boy born inside it the blessing with the longest reach.

world_behind.title: Covenants our Genesis lost
world_behind.text: Lehi quotes Joseph of Egypt's prophecies at length; surviving Genesis keeps only a trace ("God will surely visit you," Gen. 50:24). The brass plates evidently carried a fuller Joseph literature, and this chapter is the record's longest excerpt from it, another glimpse of the larger library behind the small plates.

world_behind.title: Ezekiel, writing the same doctrine that decade
world_behind.text: While Lehi blessed Joseph in the new world, Ezekiel in Babylon was joining two sticks, Judah's and Joseph's, into one (Ezek. 37:16–17). Two exiled prophets, oceans apart, drawing the same picture of two literatures becoming one testimony.

world_behind.title: Seer was the older title
world_behind.text: "A choice seer" (v. 6) reaches for the office Israel named before it named prophets (1 Sam. 9:9). A seer sees; the word claims direct sight rather than inherited text, and the record will later define the office formally (Mosiah 8:15–17) exactly as this blessing uses it.

world_behind.title: The namesake chain
world_behind.text: "His name shall be called after me; and it shall be after the name of his father" (v. 15): four Josephs stand in this chapter, the patriarch, Lehi's son, the future seer, and the seer's father. Covenant families of the age planted names like boundary stones; the repetition is memory made hereditary.

world_behind.title: Moses' mouth problem
world_behind.text: The blessing's Moses is the Exodus one precisely: power "in a rod" (v. 17), judgment "in writing" (v. 17), but with the caveat "I will not make him mighty in speaking" (v. 17), with "a spokesman" (v. 17) supplied (Ex. 4:10–16). The pattern matters because the future seer is cut to it: instruments in this tradition are deliberately incomplete.

words.text: In Jeremiah, prophesying in the city Lehi had just left, the Lord promises to "raise unto David a righteous Branch" (Jer. 23:5), a king who reigns and prospers. Joseph's prophecy reaches for the same words and then heads off the obvious reading: a righteous branch, "not the Messiah, but a branch which was to be broken off" (v. 5). The correction is the substance of the blessing. This branch is a people, snapped from the tree and carried out of sight, and everything that follows is about what will be sent to find it.

cites.quote: not the Messiah, but a branch which was to be broken off

spans.text: not the Messiah, but a branch which was to be broken off

words.text: Lehi quotes his ancestor three times in three verses and marks each lift with the same small adverb: Joseph "truly saw our day" (v. 5), "For Joseph truly testified" (v. 6), "Yea, Joseph truly said" (v. 7). The word is not filler. A father is setting his own weight behind material his sons are getting at second hand. All three marks fall in the opening lines; once the long quotation is running, Lehi lets Joseph speak unaccompanied.

words.text: To begin. The word runs seventeen times in this record and never in the King James Bible, first of the people stepping onto the path in Lehi's dream (1 Ne. 8:22). Joseph's prophecy uses it for the seer's work: "in that day when my work shall commence among all my people" (v. 13). It sits directly after the weakness and the strength, so the starting date is fixed to the moment the weak thing is made strong.

words.text: God's own lettering. The promise about Moses keeps the Exodus detail exactly: "I will write unto him my law, by the finger of mine own hand" (v. 17), which is how the tables came (Ex. 31:18). The image keeps working through the volume. Writing shows up on a temple wall at Ammonihah from the same finger (Alma 10:2), and when the veil parts for the brother of Jared the first thing he sees is a finger (Ether 3:6). In a book made by engravers, the hand of God is the hand that writes.

words.text: The dust-cry travels "according to the simpleness of their words" (v. 20): the same noun the record used for the look-and-live remedy the fathers despised (1 Ne. 17:41). Plainness in this tradition is a delivery mechanism; what the words lack in force, verse 21 supplies by faith.

words.text: "Behold, thou art little" (v. 25): the only physical detail the farewell cycle records of any son. The smallest hearer gets the longest prophecy, and his instruction is proportionate: hearken to Nephi, remember "the words of thy dying father" (v. 25). In this family the future runs through the small and the last.

phrases.text: Lehi's own name for the eight desert years, used twice in three verses. The land got named for abundance (Bountiful); the era gets named for what it cost. That the blessing born from those years reaches furthest is the chapter's quiet enactment of the consecration promise made to Jacob one chapter earlier.

The blessing's drumbeat, sounded again and again until lineage itself becomes the argument: covenants ride in bodies, through generations, regardless of exile. The phrase's repetition does what a genealogy does, but in prophecy: it keeps the line visible across a gap of centuries.

Esteemed highly, commanded narrowly, doing "a work for the fruit of thy loins" (v. 7) "of great worth unto them" (v. 7). The record here prophesies its own bringer-forth: the book quoting Joseph is the work the verse promises, the strangest and boldest loop in the volume: a text foretelling its own arrival.

phrases.text: Judah's writing and Joseph's writing, converging "unto the confounding of false doctrines and laying down of contentions" (v. 12). The verb is orchard language, not conquest language: neither literature absorbs the other; they grow into one canopy. The record's whole account of its relationship to the Bible sits in this verse.

phrases.term: Out of weakness he shall be made strong
phrases.text: The instrument-doctrine in one line, matching the epistle's formula for the faithful ("out of weakness were made strong," Heb. 11:34). Strength arrives as a change worked on weakness, not a replacement of it; the seer, the words, and the whole dust-cry of this chapter run on that conversion.

phrases.term: Cried unto them from the dust
phrases.text: The record describing its own voice: a fallen people audible only in what they wrote, "even after many generations have gone by them" (v. 20). Isaiah gave the figure its source (a voice whispering "out of the dust," Isa. 29:4), and the record adopts it as self-portrait: this book is the cry, and the reader is the brethren it was aimed at.

verses.label: v. 1–3
verses.title: A deathbed address that names its occasion twice
verses.text: The record opens the blessing by fixing when the son was born: "Thou wast born in the wilderness of mine afflictions; yea, in the days of my greatest sorrow did thy mother bear thee." Verse 3 says it again in shorter form, "whom I have brought out of the wilderness of mine afflictions." The phrase "my last-born" appears in both verses. The chapter closes at verse 25 with "Remember the words of thy dying father," so the whole passage is bracketed by statements about the speaker's own condition rather than about the son's.

verses.label: v. 4–5
verses.title: A clarification inserted to block a misreading
verses.text: The record interrupts its own promise to rule something out: the branch raised up out of Joseph's loins is "not the Messiah, but a branch which was to be broken off." Nothing in the surrounding sentence invites the confusion, and no one in the narrative has raised it. The denial is aimed at a reader, not at a hearer. Verse 4 also supplies the genealogical claim the whole chapter rests on, "I am a descendant of Joseph who was carried captive into Egypt," which the record states here and nowhere earlier.

verses.label: v. 6–8
verses.title: One phrase carrying an entire prophecy
verses.text: The record repeats "the fruit of my loins" or "the fruit of thy loins" seventeen times in this chapter, with three occurrences in verse 7 alone and three more in each of verses 12 and 18. The word "seer" appears five times. Everything the prophecy claims is attached to that one genealogical formula, so the promise concerns a line and not a place, a nation, or a throne. The phrase in that exact form occurs in no other chapter of these books; all seventeen uses are here.

verses.label: v. 12
verses.title: Two records named, with four stated purposes
verses.text: The record makes a claim about books: "the fruit of thy loins shall write; and the fruit of the loins of Judah shall write," and the two writings "shall grow together." Four outcomes follow in one sentence: confounding false doctrines, laying down contentions, establishing peace, and bringing knowledge of the fathers and of the covenants. Three of the four are corrective and one is informative. The prediction is about the relation between two texts, which makes it the sort of claim a reader can hold the finished volume to.

verses.label: v. 15
verses.title: A name given as a two-part test
verses.text: The record supplies an identification with two conditions rather than one: "his name shall be called after me; and it shall be after the name of his father." The seer must share Joseph's name and his own father's name. A prophecy that could have simply named a man instead gives a rule for recognizing him, and the rule requires two independent facts to match.

verses.label: v. 17
verses.title: A portrait of Moses built out of what he could not do
verses.text: The record describes the deliverer by limits: a rod, judgment given "in writing," and then two denials, "I will not loose his tongue, that he shall speak much," and "I will not make him mighty in speaking." The remedy is a third party, "I will make a spokesman for him." The material comes from Exodus 4:10–16, where Moses objects that he is "slow of speech" and Aaron is appointed. The record takes an episode of reluctance in the source and turns it into a permanent description of the office.

chapter.title: Four Josephs, one memory
chapter.text: Patriarch, last-born, seer, and the seer's father share a name across two and a half thousand years of this chapter's sightline. The blessing braids identity through repetition: a covenant family remembers by naming, and the name itself becomes the prophecy's carrying case.

chapter.title: The book prophesies its bringer-forth
chapter.text: The choice seer's commissioned work is the very record that preserves the prophecy about him. No bolder self-reference exists in the volume: the text stakes its credibility on a future person, named, described, and assigned to deliver it.

chapter.title: Deliverance by literature
chapter.text: Verses 9 and 10 name Moses twice and state his errand, "to deliver thy people out of the land of Egypt." Verse 11 then sets the second figure beside him with a different instrument, "unto him will I give power to bring forth my word unto the seed of thy loins," and verse 7 states the object of that errand as knowledge, "bringing them to the knowledge of the covenants which I have made with thy fathers." Two deliverers in three verses, one moving a nation and the other moving a text.

chapter.title: Convergence
chapter.text: Judah's scripture and Joseph's scripture grow together; neither is demoted. The record's theory of itself is companionship: false doctrine falls when two independent witnesses agree, and this chapter is where that theory is chartered.

chapter.title: The instrument is kept weak
chapter.text: No eloquence for Moses, no loosed tongue for the seer, simpleness for the words, and spokesmen to cover the gaps. The design is consistent and stated: power visibly God's because the instrument visibly lacks it. Weakness in this doctrine is a credential.

chapter.title: A voice from the dust
chapter.text: The chapter knows its authors will be long dead before their words land, and makes the deadness part of the message: a cry surviving its criers, aimed at descendants "after many generations" (v. 20). Few books describe their own transmission; this one mourns and exults over it in the same verse.

cites.quote: after many generations

spans.text: after many generations

chapter.title: The farewell cycle's furthest sight
chapter.text: The farewell blessings run from 2 Nephi 1 to 2 Nephi 4 and no two are alike in content. Jacob receives the fall, the atonement, and opposition across thirty verses of 2 Nephi 2. Joseph, addressed here as "my last-born" and at verse 25 as "little," receives a quoted prophecy about events in the latter days and a promise that "thy seed shall not be destroyed." The chapter closes by pointing him to a living authority rather than to the doctrine, "hearken unto the words of thy brother, Nephi."

applications.title: Name your wilderness
applications.text: Lehi called the worst years what they were, the wilderness of mine afflictions, and then identified what was born there. Do both halves: name your hardest era honestly, then list what came out of it that nothing easier would have produced.

applications.title: Bless past your sight
applications.text: Joseph of Egypt spoke usefully about descendants twenty-five centuries out. When you pray for or record blessings on your children, include the generations you will never meet; covenant words are built to outlive their speakers.

applications.title: Read the two witnesses together
applications.text: Take one doctrine this month and trace it through both records, Judah's and Joseph's, side by side. The confounding of confusion promised here happens at the seam; readers of one book only never see the agreement.

applications.title: Volunteer your weakness
applications.text: Identify the assignment you have declined because you lack the eloquence, education, or nerve for it. This chapter's whole staffing policy runs on exactly that lack: offer the weakness and let the making-strong be God's problem.

applications.title: Write for the dust
applications.text: Add something to your own record this week written explicitly for a descendant who will read it after you are gone: counsel, testimony, repentance. The chapter's authors wrote for readers whose faith they trusted before meeting them; so can you.

applications.title: Honor the little ones' blessings
applications.text: The smallest member of a family can carry its longest promises. Find the Joseph in your household, the youngest, the overlooked, and put words of specific, far-reaching blessing on them out loud.

questions.text: What was born in the days of my greatest sorrow that I have never yet credited to those days?
Where has God given me a narrow assignment I keep trying to widen, and what would doing "none other work" look like?
Do the two records actually grow together in my study, or does one of them sit shelved?
Which of my weaknesses have I hidden so well that God's making-it-strong would go unnoticed?
If my descendants could hear only what I have written down, what would my cry from the dust actually say?
Whose dying words am I charged with remembering, and when did I last act on them?
